name: Chrysoberyl
physical: Traditionally associated with a bright, vital feeling
Said to bring a sense of energy
Crystal healers link it with steady spirits
summary: Chrysoberyl is a very hard, golden-green gem and the parent of cat's eye and alexandrite, linked in crystal lore with optimism, confidence and luck.
intro: Chrysoberyl is a beryllium aluminium oxide, quite different from beryl despite the similar name. It forms stout, often twinned crystals and is one of the hardest gems after diamond and corundum. Classic colours are honey yellow, golden green and brownish yellow, with a lively, silky brilliance when well cut. Its two most famous varieties, alexandrite and cat's eye, steal most of the attention, but ordinary transparent chrysoberyl is a fine gem in its own right and tends to be great value. Tiny parallel needles give some stones a silky sheen, and those that are cut as cabochons show a floating band of light.
history: The name chrysoberyl comes from the Greek chrysos, meaning gold, and beryllos, meaning beryl, because early mineralogists saw it as a golden form of beryl. It was only recognised as a distinct mineral in the late 1700s. Sri Lanka and Brazil have been the main sources of gem-quality material for centuries, with notable finds in the Ural Mountains in the 1830s that produced alexandrite. In Victorian times chrysoberyl was popular in Georgian and Edwardian jewelry, often set in silver and gold with old-cut stones. Today it is prized by collectors who appreciate its hardness, brilliance and subtle golden glow.
meaning: In crystal tradition chrysoberyl is considered a stone of optimism, confidence and good fortune. Its golden glow links it to the solar plexus chakra, and practitioners say it helps people feel clear about their goals and brave enough to take action. It is also used for focused study, as it supports steady attention. Because it is the parent of alexandrite and cat's eye, some see it as a gateway to those stones' themes of change and protection. People use it to restore a positive outlook after disappointments. Physically it is traditionally associated with brightness and a lively feeling, as a symbolic companion rather than a remedy.
howToUse: Wear a chrysoberyl ring or pendant for confidence on important days, or carry a small stone in your pocket as a gentle reminder of your goals. In meditation, hold a golden piece over the stomach and imagine warm light growing stronger with each breath. Place it on your desk to support concentration and good decisions. Combine it with citrine for added sunniness, or with clear quartz to amplify clarity. It also works well as a lucky charm in a purse or a bag for travel.
care: Chrysoberyl is very hard and stable, so it is easy to look after. Rinse it with warm soapy water and a soft brush, and rinse and dry well. It tolerates ultrasonic cleaning in most cases if it has no fractures. Cleanse energetically with smoke, sound, moonlight or sunlight. Store each stone in a soft pouch to avoid scratching softer gems. Remove rings for rough work, as even hard stones can chip if struck hard.
identify: Chrysoberyl is hard enough to scratch quartz and topaz easily, and it feels dense. Colour ranges from yellow to green, with a bright, silky glow. Look-alikes include citrine, yellow beryl, peridot, tourmaline, apatite and glass. Chrysoberyl is rarely treated, though a few stones are heated. Cat's eye and alexandrite are separate trade names for varieties with special effects. Ask a seller to disclose any treatment and consider a lab report for expensive stones.

faq.q: Is chrysoberyl the same as beryl?
faq.a: No. Chrysoberyl is a beryllium aluminium oxide, while beryl is a beryllium aluminium silicate that includes emerald and aquamarine. The names are similar but the minerals are different.

faq.q: What are the varieties of chrysoberyl?
faq.a: The main ones are alexandrite, which changes colour, and cat's eye, which shows a bright line of light. Plain transparent chrysoberyl in yellow and green is also a lovely, durable gem.
Yes. With a hardness of 8.5 it is among the hardest gems, behind only corundum and diamond. It resists scratching and is excellent for daily jewelry.
